t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will study opiates. Opiates, by structure, are substances similar to morphine and obtained from it: morphine, codeine, heroin and its metabolite 6-monoacetylmorphine. The aim is to learn to isolate opium alkaloids from blood and urine, to detect them on TLC with Marquis and Frohde reagents, and to confirm them by UV spectrum. The plan has four parts: first, isolation; second, TLC; third, colour and microcrystalline reactions; fourth, distinguishing morphine, codeine and heroin.

As a result of the session you should be able to do the following. First, isolate opium alkaloids from blood and urine by liquid-liquid extraction. Second, distinguish the spots of morphine, codeine and heroin on TLC by Rf and by the colours with Marquis and Frohde reagents, using Table 2. Third, distinguish morphine from other opiates with iron (III) chloride. Fourth, explain that when heroin is detected, its hydrolysis products, that is monoacetylmorphine and morphine, are what is identified.

Reagents and equipment. For isolation, sodium bisulphate solution, trichloroacetic acid, 25% ammonia to bring the pH to 6.5-7.0, sodium bicarbonate, butanol-chloroform 1:9 and anhydrous sodium sulphate are needed. For TLC, a silica gel plate is taken, with the system ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia 17:2:1; solutions of morphine, codeine and heroin are used as references. The developing reagents are Marquis and Frohde; in addition, iron (III) chloride, Wagner's reagent, Reinecke's salt and 15% cadmium iodide are used.

Safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed after the work. Objects from infectious persons, that is those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents.

Classification of opium alkaloids. This group, which has narcological significance, consists mainly of opium alkaloids; they contain an isoquinoline nucleus. Isoquinoline derivatives are divided into two subgroups: phenanthrene-isoquinoline and benzyl-isoquinoline. The phenanthrene series includes morphine, codeine and thebaine. The benzyl series includes papaverine and narcotine. Opium contains more than 60 alkaloids, with a total content of up to 15-20%.

Let us distinguish opiates and opioids. Opiates: morphine, codeine, heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, and its metabolite 6-monoacetylmorphine, abbreviated 6-MAM. Opioids by chemical structure belong to another group: promedol, phencyclidine, methadone, fentanyl. Phenanthrene-isoquinoline derivatives: morphine, codeine, thebaine. Benzyl-isoquinoline derivatives: papaverine, narcotine.

Opium and omnopon. Opium is obtained from the latex of unripe opium poppy capsules; it is dark brown, with a characteristic odour and a bitter taste. Omnopon is a mixture of the hydrochloride salts of opium alkaloids, consisting of 50% morphine and 32-35% other alkaloids. Omnopon contains no meconic acid or meconin. Therefore the finding of morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid proves that opium is present in the sample.

Numbers relating to the composition of opium. Opium contains 19% morphine, 8-10% narcotine, 1.5-3% codeine, and alkaloids such as thebaine and papaverine. Opium contains more than 60 alkaloids; their total content reaches 15-20%. Meconic acid can be detected if the object contains 0.05 g of opium.

Let us compare opium and omnopon. Opium is obtained from poppy latex, is dark brown and bitter, contains more than 60 alkaloids, and has meconic acid and meconin. Omnopon is a mixture of hydrochloride salts, contains 50% morphine, and is a reddish-yellow powder; it dissolves in water at 1:15 and in ethyl alcohol at 1:50. Omnopon has no meconic acid or meconin. It is by exactly this feature that they are distinguished.

Detecting meconic acid. The biological object is acidified with HCl and soaked in ethyl alcohol, and the filtrate is evaporated to dryness. The residue is dissolved in water and boiled, MgO is added, and it is filtered hot; hydrochloric acid is added to the filtrate. With iron (III) chloride a blood-red colour forms; on heating the colour does not change.

t: Meconic acid: reaction with iron (III) chloride
n: The reaction of meconic acid with iron (III) chloride. If iron (III) chloride is added to the isolated solution, a blood-red colour forms; on heating the colour does not change. The product is an iron complex. The aqueous solution of meconic acid gives a spectral maximum at 210, 284 and 303 nm.

Meconin. Meconin in pure form is a white powder melting at 102 °C; it occurs in opium and is not used in medicine. If concentrated sulphuric acid is added to the residue, a green colour forms; on slow heating, emerald, pink and red colours are observed. If kept for two days, the colour turns red. Detection of meconin confirms that opium was consumed.

t: Metabolism of morphine, codeine and heroin
n: Metabolism of morphine, codeine and heroin. Morphine forms glucuronides: 50% is excreted in the urine in the first 8 hours, and about 90% after 24 hours. Codeine is metabolised in three directions: glucuronide, O-demethylation to morphine, and N-demethylation to norcodeine. Heroin is rapidly hydrolysed under alkaline conditions and in the body: first to monoacetylmorphine, finally to morphine.

Numbers for the metabolism and action of morphine. Morphine forms glucuronides: 50% is excreted in the urine in the first 8 hours, and about 90% after 24 hours. The smallest amount of morphine lethal to a human is 0.1-0.5 g; about 30% goes to the liver, kidneys and lungs. Euphoria is replaced by drowsiness after 30-40 minutes; the withdrawal syndrome lasts 5-7 days.

Morphine metabolites and transformation products. In conjugation, glucuronides are formed. Morphine is partly N-demethylated to normorphine and O-methylated to codeine. In cadaveric organs pseudomorphine and dihydromorphine gradually form. If oxidised in an open vessel, the stable and strongly poisonous oxidimorphine is formed; it cannot be reduced back.

The procedure for isolation from blood and urine. Sodium bisulphate is added to the sample and heated for 30 minutes on a boiling bath; it is cooled and trichloroacetic acid is added. The protein precipitate is filtered off, and the filtrate is brought to pH 6.5-7.0 with 25% ammonia. Sodium bicarbonate is added, and it is extracted twice with butanol-chloroform 1:9. It is then passed through anhydrous sodium sulphate, divided into two and evaporated.

Numbers for isolation and TLC. Sodium bisulphate is added to blood or urine and heated on a boiling water bath for 30 minutes. The filtrate is brought to pH 6.5-7.0 with 25% ammonia and extracted twice with butanol-chloroform 1:9. It has been confirmed that with this method morphine is recovered up to 83% from blood and up to 71% from urine; the detection limit is 10-15 μg.

t: Dividing the isolate into two parts
n: Dividing the isolate into two parts. The butanol-chloroform extracts are combined and passed through a filter containing anhydrous sodium sulphate. The filtrate is divided equally between two vessels and evaporated to dryness: one part for TLC, the other for additional reactions. It has been confirmed that with this method morphine can be isolated and determined up to 83% from blood and up to 71% from urine.

Performing TLC. The residue is dissolved in 0.5 ml of butanol-chloroform 1:9 and spotted on the start line of the plate; leaving a gap of 2 cm, the reference solutions are spotted. System: ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia 17:2:1; when the front has risen 10 cm, the plate is dried. From start to finish, Marquis or Frohde reagent is applied. The detection limit for morphine is 10-15 μg.

Table 2 gives the Rf and spot colours. Sorbent: silica gel; system ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia 17:2:1. The Rf values in ascending order: morphine, codeine, dionine, heroin, narcotine, papaverine. Morphine 0.32-0.39, codeine 0.39-0.52, dionine 0.41-0.46, heroin 0.52-0.66. With Marquis reagent, morphine and heroin give a red-pink spot; codeine pink, dionine blue-pink. With Frohde reagent, morphine and heroin are pink, codeine light green, dionine blue-green.

Table 3 gives the Rf values on Silufol and Sorbfil plates. In ethyl acetate-methanol-ammonia 17:2:1 on Silufol, morphine 0.20, codeine 0.40, heroin 0.52. In the same system on Sorbfil, morphine 0.27, codeine 0.49, heroin 0.65. In ether-ethanol-ammonia 6:3:1 on Silufol, morphine 0.30, codeine 0.60, heroin 0.80; on Sorbfil, morphine 0.30, codeine 0.45, heroin 0.60.

Colours with Marquis reagent. Marquis reagent is a mixture of formaldehyde and concentrated sulphuric acid; its sensitivity for codeine is 0.05 mg. A red-violet colour is given by morphine, heroin, opium, thebaine and benzylmorphine, dihydromorphine. A violet colour is seen with codeine, diamorphine, 6-monoacetylmorphine, normorphine, dihydrocodeine and others. In the table, a blue-violet colour is given for neopine, and yellow-violet for ethylmorphine and norcodeine.

Distinguishing morphine with FeCl3. With Marquis, Frohde, Mandelin and Erdmann reagents, morphine and other opium alkaloids give a violet colour. FeCl3 gives a blue-green colour with the phenolic hydroxyl of morphine; the sensitivity is low, but it is important for distinguishing. In codeine, heroin and dionine the hydrogen of the phenolic hydroxyl is substituted, so they give no colour.

t: Detecting codeine and heroin with Frohde reagent
n: Detecting codeine and heroin with Frohde reagent. Frohde reagent is a solution of ammonium molybdate in concentrated sulphuric acid; it is very characteristic for codeine, with a sensitivity of 0.1 μg. Heroin gives a violet colour with Frohde reagent just like morphine, and in this it differs from codeine. If the acetic acid formed on hydrolysis of heroin is heated with ethyl alcohol and concentrated H2SO4, an odour of ethyl acetate is given off.

Let us compare morphine and codeine. Morphine has a phenolic hydroxyl, so it gives a blue-green colour with iron (III) chloride; codeine does not. Morphine dissolves in alkali, forming a morphinate; codeine does not dissolve in alkali. The melting point of morphine base is 253-254 °C, and of codeine 153-155 °C. With Frohde reagent, morphine gives violet, while codeine gives a dirty blue, then blue-green.

Microcrystalloscopic reactions. The dry residue of the second part is dissolved in a drop of 0.1 M HCl and the reagent is added; after 10-15 minutes it is examined under the microscope. Morphine: 15% cadmium iodide gives needle-shaped crystals, limit 2.5 μg; Reinecke's salt gives pink needle-shaped crystals, 2 μg. Codeine: picrolonic acid gives yellow spherulites and white-yellow plates, 1 μg; 5% mercury (II) chloride gives needle-shaped crystals, 13 μg. Dionine forms needle-shaped and prismatic crystals; the detection limit is 14 μg.

t: Separating morphine and codeine from each other
n: Separating morphine and codeine from each other. The chloroform isolate from the alkaline medium is evaporated and an alkali solution is added to the residue. Morphine, as a morphinate, does not pass into the ether; codeine, because it does not dissolve in alkali, passes into the ether layer. Thus the ether layer is tested for codeine and the aqueous layer for morphine.

Heroin and 6-monoacetylmorphine. Heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, is synthesised from morphine by an acetylation reaction; it does not occur in opium or omnopon. In the body, in cadaveric organs and when an alkaline solution is extracted with chloroform, heroin undergoes hydrolysis. Therefore in heroin poisoning, mainly monoacetylmorphine and morphine are found in the object.

Key characteristics of heroin. The melting point of heroin as the base is 173 °C; heroin does not dissolve in water. The power of heroin to paralyse the respiratory centre is five times that of morphine. In the UV spectrum it gives a maximum at 279 nm in 0.1 M HCl and at 299 nm in 0.1 M alkali. With hexachloroplatinic acid it forms yellow needles; sensitivity 0.05-0.07 μg.

Scheme of heroin hydrolysis. Heroin is hydrolysed very rapidly under alkaline conditions and in the body. First 6-monoacetylmorphine forms, finally morphine. If the acetic acid formed in hydrolysis is heated with ethyl alcohol and concentrated H2SO4, an odour of ethyl acetate is given off.

UV spectrum maxima. A solution of morphine base in ethyl alcohol gives a maximum at 287 nm, and its solution in 0.1 M H2SO4 at 284 nm. An alcoholic solution of codeine base gives a maximum at 286 nm. Heroin 279 nm in 0.1 M HCl, 299 nm in 0.1 M alkali; and 6-monoacetylmorphine gives a maximum at 287 nm.

Dionine. Dionine is ethylmorphine hydrochloride; it does not occur in opium or omnopon and is obtained from morphine by a semi-synthetic route. Melting point 93 °C; dissolves in water at 1:12; the single maximum dose is 0.03 g. It gives no colour with iron (III) chloride; its solution in 0.2 M H2SO4 gives a maximum at 289 nm.

Methods of quantitative analysis. The quantity of morphine can be determined by a spectrophotometric method based on UV spectra. In the photocolorimetric method with the silicon-molybdate complex, a blue colour forms on adding ammonia; 0.2-4 mg of morphine is determined. The quantities of morphine, codeine and heroin are also determined by GC-MS or HPLC-MS; heroin is also determined by immunobiological methods.

Retention times in HPLC and GLC. In HPLC, the absolute retention times are: heroin 4.68, morphine 2.86, codeine 4.11 minutes. In GLC, the absolute retention times are: heroin 11.81, morphine 9.73, codeine 8.38 minutes. The table also gives UV maxima: heroin 279, morphine 281, codeine 281 nm.

Separating narcotine from morphine. If morphine is detected in the biological object, a reaction for narcotine is also carried out; since the reaction results are the same, narcotine is separated from morphine. The chloroform residue is dissolved in dilute HCl, made alkaline with NaOH and extracted with chloroform. Morphine remains as a morphinate, while narcotine passes into the extract. With concentrated H2SO4, narcotine forms a compound that is first yellow and then reddish.

Interpreting the result. If morphine is found, morphine, opium or omnopon may have been taken. Consumption of opium is proved by the finding of morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid; omnopon contains no meconic acid. Heroin is identified in the object in the form of its hydrolysis products, that is monoacetylmorphine and morphine.

Let us compare dionine, heroin and apomorphine. Dionine and heroin do not occur in opium and omnopon and are obtained from morphine by a semi-synthetic route. Dionine is ethylmorphine hydrochloride, melting point 93 °C. Heroin is diacetylmorphine, 173 °C; its power to paralyse respiration is 5 times that of morphine. Apomorphine is obtained by heating morphine under high pressure in the presence of HCl; it has two phenolic hydroxyls and oxidises quickly. It is used as an emetic; it has no analgesic or narcotic effect.

The case task is taken from the textbook. Blood was brought to the forensic chemical examination as the biological object; in the preliminary analysis the presence of morphine was suspected. Question: for which substances must the analysis be carried out? Explain the solution to the problem. The direction is as follows: if morphine is found, tests are also made for codeine, narcotine and meconic acid; if heroin is present, 6-monoacetylmorphine is sought.

Review questions. First: what is the difference between opium and omnopon? How is the identity of meconic acid determined? Second: which reactions distinguish morphine from codeine, heroin and dionine? Third: what method is used to distinguish codeine and dionine from each other? Fourth: how are opium alkaloids isolated from liquid materials?

Conclusion. Opiates are isolated from blood and urine, after heating with sodium bisulphate, by extraction with butanol-chloroform 1:9. On TLC, Rf and the colours with Marquis and Frohde reagents, FeCl3 and microcrystals distinguish morphine, codeine and heroin. The UV spectrum confirms; the quantity is determined by UV, photocolorimetry, GC-MS or HPLC-MS.
